title: How many switches untie a trefoil?
hook: Switch a crossing and its top strand goes under. How many until the knot falls open?

knows: a knot is a closed loop drawn with over and under crossings
doesNotKnow: that switching one crossing (the top strand goes under) can free a knot, because after the switch a strand lies on top at two crossings in a row and can slide off; and that on the trefoil and the figure-eight any one switch does it

misconception: To untie a knot you must undo every crossing, or find the one special crossing to switch.
objective: The learner can explain that one switch frees the trefoil whichever crossing it is, because after the switch a strand lies on top twice in a row and slides off.
keyState: Trefoil tally 3 of 3: each of the trefoil's three crossings, switched alone, gave a plain loop (milestones 'firstFree' then 'allThree'; the tally survives Reset and chip changes).

claims.text: Switching a crossing makes its top strand go under: it exchanges which strand is over and which is under there (hook 'Switch a crossing and its top strand goes under'; question 'Switching a crossing makes its top strand go under').

No crossing was special.').

The stage readout reads simplify status only. Builder-written; unverified.

claims.text: After any single switch of the kit's trefoil (or figure-eight), one strand lies on top at both crossings of a two-sided gap, so it can slide off (a Reidemeister II move); the unswitched drawings have no such place (tinted strand; caption 'On top twice: it slides off'; reveal 'After each switch, the tinted strand lay on top at two crossings in a row, so it slides off').
claims.source: moves(q) on src/kit/knots, read only: after each single switch the first R2 contains the tapped crossing, one of its two edges is in an over slot of the PD tuple at both of its crossings and the other is under at both (7 of 7); unswitched 3_1 and 4_1 offer no R2. Brief checks K15 and K20 (node company/domains/briefs/checks/knots-check.mjs); builder probe 2026-10-16: 3_1 switch 0 R2 [0,1] edges [4,1] over-at-both 1; switch 1 R2 [0,1] edge 4; switch 2 R2 [0,2] edge 5; 4_1 switch 0 R2 [0,2] edge 5; 1 R2 [1,3] edge 7; 2 R2 [0,2] edge 1; 3 R2 [1,3] edge 3. Brief claim 3. Builder-written; unverified.

claims.text: On the switched trefoil, after the strand slides off, the twist left over falls out: one crossing is left and it is a kink that undoes with a Reidemeister I move (reveal 'and the twist left over falls out').
claims.source: Builder probe 2026-10-16 on src/kit/knots (numbers only, never drawn): apply the first R2 to each single switch of 3_1 -> 1 crossing left, moves offers R1, after it 0 crossings (3 of 3); on 4_1 -> 2 crossings left, R1 then R1 (4 of 4). Design note company/reviews/unknot-game/design.md marks this clause as told context. Builder-written; unverified.

claims.text: The unknotting number of a knot is the fewest crossing switches, over all drawings of it, that turn it into a plain loop; it is 1 for the trefoil and for the figure-eight (reveal 'The fewest switches that can free a knot is its unknotting number: 1 for the trefoil, and for the figure-eight too.'; prediction answer '1').
claims.source: Adams, The Knot Book, chapter on unknotting number (citation for the definition; fact-checker to confirm chapter and wording). Value 1: one switch frees each kit drawing (c3, brief check K9 also reads table u=1 for 3_1 and 4_1), and a knotted diagram needs at least one. Brief claim 4. 'and for the figure-eight too' is claimed context unless 4_1 was visited; brief cut order puts it second. Builder-written; unverified.

claims.text: Some knots need more than one switch to become a plain loop (reveal 'Some knots need more than one.'). Example for the fact-checker, not in learner text: the (2,7) torus knot has unknotting number 3.
claims.source: Brief claim 5: Brittenham and Hermiller, arXiv 2506.24088 (research note company/research/notes/2026-10-13-teachable-knot-theory.md §2.7, high; full text unchecked). Builder note for the fact-checker, not checked: the torus-knot value is also the Milnor conjecture, proved by Kronheimer and Mrowka (1993). Brief cut order: cut this sentence first if unchecked. Builder-written; unverified.

recall.question: A knot drawing has 5 crossings. Switching any one of them gives a plain loop. How many switches did you need to free it?
recall.why: Any single switch frees it, so one is enough, whichever crossing you pick. No crossing is special, and you never need to undo them all.
